q: A second-year machining student compares the degrees, apprenticeships and NIMS credentials that lead to a CNC programmer job and notes the algebra and geometry she still needs. She is determining:
o: academic knowledge and skills required for postsecondary education and careers
e: Know the requirements before choosing a path.

q: A student planning a career in CNC programming should take courses in:
e: CNC careers rely on these skills.

q: A shop owner explains that customers expect on-time delivery, parts to print and quick answers when a problem arises. Meeting these expectations helps to:
A machinist who finds that a batch will be late should:
o: tell the supervisor right away so the customer can be notified

q: A student practices a mock job interview, completes an application and writes a resume listing her NIMS credentials. She is demonstrating standards required in the workplace such as:
o: interviewing, completing applications and resume writing

q: A good resume for a machinist apprenticeship should list:
o: skills, training and relevant projects or credentials

q: Each semester a student checks which NIMS credentials she has earned against the list she set in ninth grade and updates her plan. She is evaluating:
Reviewing progress toward a career goal helps a student:
o: adjust the plan and stay on track

o: clarify objectives and expectations in the workplace

q: When a print revision is unclear, the machinist should:
o: ask the engineer or supervisor before cutting

q: A CNC shop posts its lockout/tagout procedure, requires hearing protection near the loud saws and keeps safety data sheets handy. These show skills related to:
o: health and safety in the workplace as specified by OSHA

q: A technician is about to clear a jam inside a CNC cell. To keep anyone from restarting the equipment while her hands are inside, she should:
o: ask a coworker to watch the start button
apply her own lock and tag to the energy source

q: A machinist uses tables in the handbook to find the tap drill for a 5/16-18 thread and the allowance for a class 2 fit. She is applying:
o: technical aspects found in The Machinery's Handbook
e: The handbook provides threads and fits data.

q: A machinist needs the minor diameter of a standard thread. The best source is:
e: Thread data is in the handbook.

q: A student searches a tooling supplier's website for insert recommendations and checks the source is a reputable manufacturer. She is selecting:
o: appropriate Internet resources as applied to manufacturing

q: A reliable Internet source for the cutting speed of a particular insert grade is:

o: a detailed turning part such as the NIMS Level 1 turning project

q: The NIMS credential is useful to a machinist because it:
o: proves skills against an industry standard

q: A student mills a plate with a pocket, a bolt-hole pattern and a contour to NIMS Level 1 print dimensions and inspects each feature. She is developing:
o: a detailed milling part such as the NIMS Level 1 milling part

q: A NIMS-style milling project is graded mainly on:
o: how it looks in a photo
how closely the part matches the print tolerances

q: A student researches how punched tape and early servo controls led to modern computer-controlled machines. She is researching:
o: the history of numerical control machines

q: Early numerical control machines were commonly programmed using:
A class tours a plant and sees a 2-axis lathe, a 3-axis vertical mill, a wire EDM and a laser cutter all running programs. They are distinguishing among:
o: different types of CNC machines used in industry

q: A wire EDM machine is used to:
o: cut hard metals using electrical sparks and a wire

o: the methods by which programs can be entered into a control
e: Programs can be entered several ways.

q: One way to enter a CNC program at the machine is:
e: MDI types commands at the control.

q: A student labels a drawing with the terms spindle, turret, work offset, feed rate and G-code to build her shop vocabulary. She is using:
o: appropriate machining terminology to enhance CNC vocabulary

q: The rate at which the cutter or workpiece advances during cutting is the:
e: Feed rate = travel per time or per revolution.

q: A student studies the servo motors and ball screws that move the axes of a CNC mill and how the stepper motors on a small router differ. She is examining:
o: the types of drive motors used on CNC machinery
e: Servo and stepper drives move axes.

q: Compared with stepper motors, servo motors on a CNC machine typically provide:
A student explains that every point on a flat part can be located by an X distance and a Y distance from the origin and shows it on a graph. She is explaining:
e: Cartesian coordinates use axes from an origin.

q: On a CNC mill, the point at coordinates X2, Y3 lies:
o: 2 units along X and 3 units along Y from the origin
3 units along X and 2 along Y

In incremental positioning, each move is measured from:

o: errors do not stack from one feature to the next
e: Each feature is located from the same datum.

q: A student writes out which tools, speeds, feeds and cutting order she will use to machine an aluminum bracket and then labels each operation. She is developing:
o: a detailed process plan including tool selection, feeds and speeds
e: A process plan guides CNC programming.

q: A detailed CNC process plan should be completed:
A student arranges the operations so that roughing comes before finishing and plans in-process checks of the critical bore. She is developing:
o: a logical sequence of operations and appropriate inspection points

q: Roughing cuts are usually done before finishing cuts because:
o: they remove most material and leave stock for the final pass

q: A student mounts a triangular carbide insert on a holder, tightens the screw and runs a turning pass. She is demonstrating the use of:
e: Carbide inserts are common cutting tools.

q: A key advantage of carbide inserts is that they:
o: stay hard at high cutting speeds

q: A machinist chooses an insert's shape, grade, nose radius and coating after checking the catalog for the material to be cut. She is applying:
o: carbide inserts by determining the correct type, grade and geometry
e: Match the insert to the job.

q: A larger nose radius on a turning insert generally gives:
o: a stronger tip but more cutting pressure

q: A student swaps from a drill to a 1/2-inch end mill to a face mill by hand and by using the machine's automatic changer. She is performing:
e: Tool changes are manual or automatic.

q: Before changing a tool manually on a CNC mill, the operator should first:
o: open the guard during a cut
stop the spindle and make sure the machine is in a safe state

q: A class installs collet-style tool holders that can be exchanged in the spindle in seconds without re-measuring each tool. They are demonstrating:
o: quick change tooling used on CNC milling machines

A tool length offset tells the control:
o: how far the tool tip extends from the spindle

q: A student touches off a tool on the part's surface and records the Z value to find that tool's length offset. She is determining:
To measure a tool's length offset, an operator commonly:
o: touches the tool to a known surface and records the Z position

q: A student enters work and tool offsets for each of three tools and runs a first part to confirm the dimensions. She is incorporating:
After entering offsets for a new setup, the operator should:
o: run the first part carefully and verify its dimensions

q: Before running a CNC lathe, a student closes the chuck guard, checks that the jaws are tight on the bar and keeps the door interlock working. She is using:
o: equipment commonly associated with a CNC lathe in a safe manner

q: The chuck pressure on a CNC lathe is checked so that the workpiece:
o: does not come loose at spindle speed

q: A student points to the spindle, chuck, turret, tailstock and operator panel on a CNC lathe and explains what each does. She is recognizing, naming and describing:
o: the primary components of a CNC lathe

q: On a CNC lathe, the turret is the component that:
o: holds several tools and indexes the right one into position

q: At the start of each shift a student checks the way lube level, the hydraulic pressure and the air pressure on the CNC lathe. She is performing:
o: preventative maintenance checks on a CNC lathe

q: Checking the way lube on a CNC lathe each day helps to:
o: prevent wear and keep the slides moving smoothly

q: A student uses a refractometer to check the coolant mix on the lathe and adds concentrate when the reading is low. She is testing:
o: the coolant for proper density and adjusting it

q: A tool used to measure the concentration of water-soluble coolant is a:

o: a restart of a laptop only
a power up on a standard CNC lathe

o: home the axes before running a program

q: A student uses the handwheel and jog keys to move the turret toward the part in small steps until it nearly touches the stock. She is demonstrating:
o: the use of jog controls on the operator panel of a CNC lathe

q: When jogging a tool close to a part, the operator should use:
o: a slow jog speed or small handwheel increments

q: A student assembles a boring bar in its holder, sets the stickout and measures it on a presetter before loading it into the turret. She is demonstrating the ability to:
o: locate, assemble and measure tooling for a CNC lathe

q: The stickout of a boring bar is kept short because a long overhang:
o: can cause chatter and poor accuracy

q: A student loads each turned-part tool into its numbered turret pocket to match the tool list in the program. She is:
o: installing tools and holders in the automatic tool changer locations of a CNC lathe
e: Tool numbers must match the program.

q: If a tool is placed in the wrong turret position, the machine may:
o: use the wrong tool and crash

q: A student touches the tool to the face of the bar stock and sets that Z position as the part's face zero on the lathe. She is:
o: locating and setting the workpiece to zero on a CNC lathe
e: Z zero is commonly the part face.

q: On many CNC lathe programs, the Z zero is set at:
o: the finished face of the part

q: After touching off, the student enters the work offset in G54 so the program references the part instead of the machine origin. She is setting:
o: work offsets for the part to be machined

q: A work offset such as G54 tells the control:
o: where the part's zero is relative to the machine

q: For each turning, boring and threading tool in the turret, the student enters the X and Z geometry values that the control uses to place the tool tip. She is setting:
o: the proper geometry/tool offsets for each tool in a standard tool turret

q: If a tool's offset is entered incorrectly, the finished part will most likely:
o: have the wrong size or the tool may crash

q: After proving out the program in single-block mode, the operator presses cycle start and lets the lathe run through all the operations by itself. She is operating:
o: a CNC lathe in automatic mode

q: While a CNC lathe runs in automatic mode, the operator should:
o: stay at the machine and watch for problems

q: At the end of the shift, the student retracts the turret, cleans the chips, presses the power-off button and flips the main disconnect. She is illustrating:
o: the proper power down process on a CNC lathe

q: Before powering down a CNC lathe, the operator should first:
o: cut the main power at once
return the axes to a safe position and clean the machine

q: A student checks that the vise is tight, the spindle is stopped and the enclosure door is closed before pressing cycle start on a CNC mill. She is using:
o: equipment commonly found on and around a CNC mill in a safe manner

q: Before starting a CNC mill program, the operator should confirm that the:
o: workholding is secure and the area is clear

q: A student points to the column, table, spindle, tool changer and control on a vertical machining center and explains each. She is recognizing, naming and describing:
o: the primary components of a CNC mill

q: On a CNC mill, the automatic tool changer is the component that:
o: swaps tools in and out of the spindle during a program

q: Before a mill job, an operator checks the oil in the way lubrication reservoir, the air pressure and the spindle taper for chips. She is performing:
o: preventative maintenance checks on a CNC mill

q: Keeping the spindle taper clean on a CNC mill helps to:

o: the coolant for proper density and adjusting it

q: Coolant that is too weak in concentration can cause:

o: a power up on a standard CNC mill

q: The homing routine on a CNC mill is run to:
A student uses the jog dial on the pendant to move the table in X and Y until the cutter sits just above the corner of the part. She is demonstrating:
o: the use of jog controls on a CNC mill

q: The Z axis on a vertical mill is the axis that moves:

o: locate, assemble and measure tooling for a CNC mill

q: A tool presetter is used to:
o: measure a tool's length and diameter off the machine

q: A student loads each cutter into its numbered pocket in the tool magazine so each matches the T number in the program. She is:
o: installing tools and holders in the automatic tool changer locations of a CNC mill

q: If tool 5 in the program is loaded in pocket 6 of the magazine, the likely result is that:
o: the wrong tool will be used

q: A student uses an edge finder to locate the left and front edges of a plate in the vise and sets those as X zero and Y zero. She is:
o: locating and setting a workpiece to zero on a CNC mill

q: An edge finder helps an operator to:
o: locate the edge of a part to set zero

o: work offsets for the part to be machined

q: Using G55 instead of G54 in a program means the control uses:

o: the proper geometry/tool offsets for each tool in a standard tool-changer

q: If a mill's tool length offset is too short, the tool will:
o: stop above the part and cut too shallow

o: a CNC mill in automatic mode

o: the proper power down process on a CNC mill

q: Before powering down a CNC mill, the operator should:
o: clean the machine and move the axes to a safe position

o: trigonometry to determine coordinates from technical drawings for a CNC lathe

o: the same as its Z length

o: appropriate mathematical skills to solve problems while programming a CNC lathe

o: a simple program to face and turn

o: the X axis toward the centerline

o: program the part's profile instead of the tool's center

o: a program using canned cycles such as G71

e: G71 is a stock removal cycle.

o: a program and producing a complex part such as a NIMS Level 1 CNC turning project

o: simulate it and run it in single-block mode

o: trigonometry to determine coordinates from technical drawings for a CNC mill

o: appropriate mathematical skills to solve problems while programming a CNC mill

o: RPM by chip load per tooth by number of teeth

o: a simple program to perform hole operations

e: G81 is a simple drilling cycle.

o: a simple program to cut radiuses and angles

o: reduce tool stress and give a smoother entry
